quotes.verbatim_quote:
Open String Chords
We could say that the open string chords are the beginning and the ending path to learning
guitar chords. When we start playing, the 7irst thing we learn are the basic open string
chords such as "C" major, "E" major, "A"minor and so on. However, as soon as we have more
knowledge, we understand that they can be much more than just simple chords. Actually,
this type of chord family will create clusters that we cannot play without using at least one
open string.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines what open string chords are and why they matter at both beginner and advanced levels, framing the entire chapter's scope.

quotes.topic: Two types of open string chords
quotes.verbatim_quote:
How to Find the Open String Chord Possibilities:
Despite seeming to be very dif7icult to memorize and learn, the process to 7ind the open
string chord possibilities all over the guitar neck is quite simple to understand and apply.
There are 2 types of open string chords.

A) Chords that can only be played in a determined key and there is no possibility to create
   the same chord voicing in other keys.
B) Chords that can be played in many other keys, using the same chord voicing but losing
   all the open strings.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Establishes the two-category taxonomy that organizes all subsequent chord shape exploration in the chapter.

quotes.why_load_bearing: States the core technique rule: move any shape to different frets while keeping at least one string open, and identifies which open strings are most common.

quotes.topic: Step-by-step process: choose and apply shapes
quotes.verbatim_quote:
Step 1:
Choose a chord shape leaving at least one open string.

Step 2:
After choosing the shape, apply it on every fret, thus analysing and checking what the best
sounding possibilities are. As a matter of fact, as time goes by we do not have to apply this
process everytime, because we will memorize which options are best and apply them in
the songs we know. It is important to understand that some open string chords might
repeat some of the notes within it. But sometimes the doubled notes can give an amazing
effect, mainly when we are playing arpeggios.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Provides the two-step method for discovering open string chord possibilities, including the insight that doubled notes can be a feature rather than a flaw when playing arpeggios.

quotes.topic: Chords that change identity by fret
quotes.verbatim_quote:
As mentioned before, we can get a chord shape that we know, leaving at least 1 open string,
applying it over the other frets of the guitar fretboard. We will 9ind amazing possibilities,
but it is important to understand that some chords do not change their characteristics, but
others can change completely, going from a major chord to a minor chord at times.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Warns the student that sliding a shape up the neck can fundamentally alter the chord quality — a critical conceptual rule for safe application of the method.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Pedal point, also known as pedal tone or pedal note, is a sustained note while other notes
  are moving. Usually, we use this concept to create a sequence of chords using the same
  bass note.

  However, we can use a pedal point to create sequences of chords that have the same note
  on the top. We call this an "inverted pedal". In addition to using this concept on the lower
  and higher notes, we can still use it for notes between the bass and the upper notes.

  This concept has been used since the early baroque era, and works to create tension in the
  harmony, breaking the monotony of common chords. On the guitar, we often use bass
  pedal points using open strings. We can apply it using the D, A or E strings. However, we
  can use what we call drop "D" tunning, which is tunning the E string into "D".
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines pedal point, inverted pedal, and inner pedal in one passage, and names the specific open strings used for guitar bass pedal points, including Drop D tuning.

quotes.topic: How to use pedal point chords
quotes.verbatim_quote:
The best way to use the pedal point chords or any open string chord, is to apply them as much
  as you can in every situation that is possible. It is advisable to apply them using simple and
  short sequences such as:

  1) I, IVm           2) I, VI, IIm, V               3) IV, IVm, I                  4) I, V
quotes.why_load_bearing: Gives the practical rule for how to begin applying pedal point and open string chords in a musical context, with four specific short harmonic sequence templates.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The blues teaches us how to “tell a story" through melodies and with improvisation, similar
     to question and answer by having an extremely organized structure, being easy and
     didactic to understand. It is the perfect place to start for those who wish to learn any style,
     melodically, harmonically and rhythmically speaking.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Articulates the pedagogical rationale for beginning with the blues as a universal entry point for melody, harmony, and rhythm across all styles.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The blues can have many harmonic variations, but let’s learn the most common ones. On
     the next pages we have two different Blues Forms (2 Major and 2 Minor), presented with
     roman numerals, which deDine the degrees to memorize and to distinguish them from each
     other. Snap your Dingers on beats 2 and 4, similar to what the drummer plays on the hi hat,
     then sing the degrees of each one of the shown blues forms. This is a very important step
     because we must know these forms inside and out without having to think about them.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Prescribes a specific practice technique — snapping on beats 2 and 4 while singing scale degrees — as the mandatory method for internalizing blues form progressions.
